Chapter 2

A first look under the hood.

When we understand how the car works, we can start driving better.

A model and a harness are two different things.

People use the words interchangeably. They shouldn’t.

The model

Guesses the next token from all the tokens that came before it. That’s all it does.

The harness

What sits on top of the model: the system prompt, the tools it may use, the interface you see.

The model does one thing: guess the next token.

Whatever it makes, it’s all letters and numbers.

They just happen to form an image, a presentation, an HTML page.

The harness sits on top of the model. Claude has three.

Chat, Cowork and Code: three distinct harnesses, one model family underneath.

Chat

Conversations, artifacts, memory

Cowork

Your files, connectors, scheduled tasks

Code

Your repo, your terminal, git

Anthropic model

Opus, Sonnet, Haiku. The same family underneath all three.

The harness hands the model its tools

Through a system prompt: “when you do this, you may use these.” Three you see every day:

Read

Pulls an entire file into the model’s context. That’s all it does.

Edit

Makes a modification to that file: red to green.

Bash

Runs commands: save the file, make a folder for it.

“The button should be green.” Three tools, one fix.

The model asks for a tool, the harness runs it, the result comes back.

Today’s example: a small 90s-style shooter, built from scratch.

A boomer shooter: fast, simple, runs in the browser. Low stakes on purpose.

pickups, secrets

A game is the ideal playground: every tool gets tried, and nothing breaks that matters.

This prompt steers Claude to these tools without naming one

“Let’s create a boomer shooter together, let’s prototype a small game. Spin up a few sonnet-class subagents that research old-school boomer shooters. What made them fun? What made them succeed or fail? Put those findings into an easy-to-read, visual document that I can share with others. Do not implement the game yet.”

Multi-step work: a task list you can follow

WebSearch · WebFetch

Chapter 3

Skills.

The next part of the car. What if you want to do that research again, for another project?

The barest definition:

A skill is a reusable prompt.

Turn the boomer shooter research into a skill

So the next research job follows the same standard approach, in any domain.

my prompt

“Let’s convert this research workflow into a skill so I can reuse it later for other projects. The skill should be agnostic in that it can be used in any setting, not only games.”

parallel-research-brief/SKILL.md

name: parallel-research-brief

description: Use when asked to research a topic with several parallel subagents and turn the findings into a visual, shareable document (any domain: products, markets, tech, games, history).

1  Frame the question: subject, lens, purpose, audience

2  Open the document skeleton first

3  Dispatch 3 parallel subagents: fundamentals, success vs failure, current state

4  Fill the document, one section per write

5  Verify the visuals and finish

I never asked for /skill-creator. Claude picked it.

Claude ships with a skill that creates skills. Its description told the model this was the right tool for the job.

“Use when” decides whether a skill triggers

You’ll find it in every model-invokable skill. It tells the model what to listen for.

skill-creator · description

Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill’s description for better triggering accuracy.

parallel-research-brief · description

Use when asked to research a topic with several parallel subagents and turn the findings into a visual, shareable document (any domain: products, markets, tech, games, history).

disable-model-invocation decides who may trigger it

The second most important frontmatter field. It’s false by default.

deploy-staging/SKILL.md

---
name: deploy-staging
description: Use when deploying the
  current branch to staging
disable-model-invocation: true
---

false  default

Claude may trigger it on its own when the “use when” matches. Good for research, docs, conventions.

true

Only runs when you type /deploy-staging yourself. Use it for anything with side effects: deploys, releases, sending messages.

Chapter 4

Sharing skills.

A skill is a folder. Folders are easy to hand to a colleague.

A skill is a folder, and SKILL.md is only the first file in it

Put pretty much anything you like next to it. Claude opens the rest only when a step needs it.

a skill folder

research-brief/
  SKILL.md        always, once invoked
  references/
    doc-outline.md
  scripts/
    check_sources.py
  assets/
    timeline-template.svg

SKILL.md

The instructions. Loaded as soon as the skill triggers.

Extra markdown

Longer references Claude reads only when a step needs them.

Scripts and assets

Code Claude can run, templates, boilerplate. They don’t cost context until used.

Someone made a skill and shared it. Two ways to get it.

The same two ways work for the skills you make and want to hand to your team.

Through Claude

Lives in your subscription, so it follows you across Chat, Cowork and Code.

With the skills npm package

$ npx skills add [owner/repo]

Project, lands in the repository, shared with everyone who clones it

<project>/.claude/skills/research-brief/

User, lands in your home folder, available in every project

~/.claude/skills/research-brief/

Did something you’ll reuse? Wrap it in a skill

It’s token-efficient, it saves a ton of time, and you can update a skill whenever you want to add features or refine it. Three of mine:

/cinematic-motion-deck

You’re looking at it

Layout and animation for this deck. It’s not responsible for the content.

/notes-to-shareable-pdf

Turns my handwritten Notion notes into Faktion-branded PDFs, without the usual Claude-isms.

/jira-ticket-writer

my most-used

Turns my transcribed audio into tickets in a structured format and sends them to Atlassian.

None of these three write code. Skills are for anything you do twice.

Chapter 5

CLAUDE.md.

The instructions Claude reads before you type a word.

CLAUDE.md is the first place the harness looks

The entry point for context, definitions and instructions in a project.

CLAUDE.md

# Project
Next.js app, API routes live in src/api.

## Commands
- Run tests: pnpm test
- Lint: pnpm lint

## Conventions
- Store all dates in UTC

Loaded into every session

It’s part of the context before you type anything.

Lives in the repo root

Commit it, and the whole team gets the same context.

Personal rules too

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to all your projects.

Without CLAUDE.md, Claude explores first

You say “run the tests”. Claude doesn’t know how, so it looks.

Read("package.json")

Reads the file into context.

thinking

“There’s a test script. Probably pnpm test.”

Bash("pnpm test")

Runs the tests.

2 tool calls

plus the tokens to read package.json

With one line in CLAUDE.md, it goes straight to the test run

A few tokens saved per run. Multiply that across every test run and every kind of instruction, and you might save yourself a usage window every month.

Bash("pnpm test")

Runs the tests. No exploration step.

CLAUDE.md

- Run tests: pnpm test

1 tool call

and no file read to pay for

It’s still an instruction, and Claude can choose to ignore it

Every now and then it skips the line and explores anyway. That’s fine for some rules, and not for others.

Fine as an instruction

You can run tests with pnpm test
Store all dates in UTC

Not fine as an instruction

Always run the tests after every session
Never force-push a branch

Write it for the first kind. The second kind needs something the model can’t skip.

Hooks enforce behavior

The scenario: tests must run before the agent hands the turn back to you.

what Claude sees

1

A small code edit, and “done.”

From the agent’s point of view the work is finished.

> make the primary button green
⏺ Update(dashboard.html)
⎿ Updated 1 line
⏺ Done. The button is green now.

2

That fires a Stop event. We hook in and run the tests.

The harness runs them. The agent didn’t choose this and can’t skip it.

Stop run-tests.sh running pnpm test…

3

The test output lands straight in the context.

Two failures, and they’re the next thing the agent reads.

✕ 2 failed exit 2, output sent back to Claude
button.contrast: expected #1A7F37, got #22C55E
button.hover: expected a darker shade

4

It sees why, fixes it, then hands the turn back to you.

You never saw the red build. Nobody had to remember the rule.

∴ The contrast test wants the darker green.
⏺ Update(dashboard.html)
Stop run-tests.sh ✓ 48 passed
⏺ Done. Button is green, tests pass.

A hook is one setting and one script, in the repository.

Commit both, and everyone who clones the project gets the same guardrail.

.claude/settings.json

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": ".claude/hooks/run-tests.sh"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

.claude/hooks/run-tests.sh

#!/bin/bash
# runs every time Claude wants to finish
pnpm test 1>&2 || exit 2

# exit 2: the test output goes back to
# Claude, and it has to keep working

Other moments: before a tool runs, after a tool runs, when a prompt comes. Documentation can be found here

Chapter 6

Alignment.

Agreeing on the destination before the car moves. Making sure Claude builds what you actually mean.

Alignment is the skill to get good at as AI writes more of our code

Before

20% AI, basic ways

80% writing code ourselves

Today

Most of the code is generated

us

The more code is generated, the more it matters that we agreed on what to build first.

Introducing Grill Me

Probably the most important skill in my kit today. It’s a very simple prompt:

“Grill the user relentlessly until a shared understanding is met.”

Most harnesses have a built-in plan mode. It asks a few questions and then runs.

Grill me stops you at every gap, and only then does the work start. You’re back in control.

Grill me stops you in the gaps the agent would have filled

Here’s what that looks like for our boomer shooter

Grill me, scoped

/grill-me on game design only. I don’t care about the technical side this time.

It read the doc first

And flagged a conflict: the doc said Godot, I asked for Three.js.

Questions in rounds

Round 1 only covers what doesn’t depend on anything else.

Every question has a recommendation

Accept it, or pick from real options with trade-offs.

Grill me works through a frontier of open questions

A frontier is a set of questions. After each round, the next round is calculated from the answers.

Make /grill-me the first step of your daily workflow

When I pick up a ticket, my prompt usually looks like this:

> Let’s implement AH-181 together, /grill-me before implementing the feature

1

Reads the ticket

Pulls in the context of AH-181.

2

Applies it to the codebase

Finds where the change lands and what it touches.

3

Aligns with you

Grills you on the gaps before a single line is written.

It dramatically improves the output for the ticket, especially when the ticket itself is written well.

The entire Skills Framework around grill-me is public

I highly recommend giving it a look.

Start your journey at

aihero.dev

written by Matt Pocock

Every grill message lands in the context window

On every call, Claude Code sends all of it again, plus tools, skills and CLAUDE.md.

Grill, implement, and the context window fills up

The more tokens in the window, the less reliable each next token becomes.

The style meter made it in

A playable v0.1

One looping level, a kill counter, health, armor, shells.

Now let’s make it better

The recipe, so you can do this on Monday

From an idea to a first version. Five steps, each one a skill you type, each one leaves a file behind.

1

Research

/research what made boomer shooters fun

Cited sources, not opinions.

→ research.md

2

Grill

/grill-me

It asks until nothing is left. You answer. This is where you decide.

→ the decisions

3

Spec and tickets

/to-spec
/to-tickets

The conversation becomes a spec. The spec becomes small tickets.

→ SPEC.md, tickets

4

Build and test

/implement

Ticket by ticket. The Stop hook runs the tests whether it likes it or not.

→ code, green tests

5

Try it, grill again

/code-review
/grill-me on what’s wrong

Use the thing. What annoys you becomes the next round.

→ v0.2

All five are in Matt’s repo. Step 2 is the only one where you have to think. The handout has the prompts.

Aligned, and running.

Now build it the same way every time.

Chapter 7

The factory.

One skill, many agents, the same run every time. Improving the game without sitting next to it.

Everyone vibe-codes differently. A factory runs the same way for everyone.

Vibe coding

One person, one chat, one style.

Fast to a prototype, slow to a second one that matches.

Review and tests happen if someone remembers.

The reasoning lives in a transcript nobody reopens.

Vibe engineering

An aligned spec goes in.

Fixed phases: research, contract, build, review, test.

Review and security checks are steps, not favours.

A report comes out that anyone can read.

The factory is just a skill. Install it, and ten people get the same run.

One skill turns Claude into the director

“You are the director and integrator, not the only builder.”

orchestrated-game-dev/SKILL.md

1

Decide

Audit the build, then named design passes. Every pass must cut something.

2

Contract

Lock the spec, write the contracts, build the core and pre-wire every agent’s file.

3

Build in parallel

Subagents with exclusive file ownership, each verifying in its own browser tab.

4

Verify

Review every handback yourself. Smoke tests, perf, A/B sims against the backup.

Automatic or manual: the same factory, you choose who directs

Automatic

The orchestrator decides at every gate: what to build, what passes review, when it’s done.

You read the report at the end.

For a redesign, a prototype, a throwaway experiment.

Manual

You are the orchestrator. The factory stops at each gate and hands you the artifacts: the design passes, the research, the review findings, the prototype.

Nothing moves until you say so.

For anything a client will see or that touches production.

Same skill, same phases, same report. The toggle is who approves.

When words stop aligning people, ask for an artifact

Grill me aligns you with Claude. An artifact aligns you with everyone who doesn’t read the transcript.

orchestrator, locked contracts, exclusive file ownership, A/B sims with n ≥ 8

The factory is one skill and one prompt

Nothing in it is new. It’s the recipe from the alignment chapter, run by an orchestrator instead of by you, with subagents doing the typing.

The start prompt, more or less

“Use the orchestrated-game-dev skill on this repo. Manual mode. Audit the current build, propose the design passes, and stop at every gate until I approve.”

Swap “game” for your project. The skill is a folder with a SKILL.md and a few reference files. You can read it in ten minutes.

stage

who runs what

Research

subagents, each running /research

Tickets

subagents, /to-tickets

Design

an artifact, your feedback, until approved

Grill

/grill-me per ticket, you answer

Implement

subagents, /implement, one owns one file

Review and QA

/code-review, playtest agents, one report

Every stage is one of Matt’s skills, or one you wrote. The orchestrator only briefs, reads what comes back, and stops at the orange rows. A generalised version, /orchestrated-build, is in the talk’s repo.

Chapter 8

Automated QA.

We built it. An agent can see, hear and play the game on its own. So let it play as someone else.

Give an agent a persona and let it playtest

The veteran

hands: expert

Plays boomer shooters for a living and knows exactly what he’s doing.

Wants a thrilling but challenging experience.

asks

“Which deaths were fair?”

“Is any fight trivial, or a wall?”

The graphics guy

hands: casual

Hardly ever plays games. Has an eye for visuals.

Wants a fair and fun time, nothing more.

asks

“Would I come back tomorrow?”

“When did I get annoyed?”

In round 1 these were Rhea, the challenge seeker, and Mila, the cozy casual, in a panel of 7 from the skill’s library of 14.

Each persona is a brain with bot hands

LLMs can’t twitch, but they judge choices, clarity, feel and fairness well. 40 game-seconds ran in 82 ms.

hands

FPS bot, written for OVERTIME

Aims with reaction delay and noise, strafes, dashes through sniper shots, routes to pickups.

brain

The persona picks the tactics

Stance, preferred weapon, target priority, pickup greed, when to heal, when to rush for a Termination.

A/B test of a fix

Patched the rescue rule for stuck enemies, then re-ran the batches.

5/8 → 0/8

stalled runs on deck stance. Median wave 26, up from 15. Normal play unchanged.

Then reverted: the decision stays with the team.

What round 1 found

1

Burnouts are the biggest problem

35% of damage, 36% of deaths. Their death blast hurts whoever kills them.

2

Wave 2 is a wall for new players

Half the casual runs died there, right after a 12-second wave 1.

3

Waves can stall forever

Enemies can’t climb stairs. A tested fix removes the stalls.

4

Deaths teach nothing

A joke reason, no cause. Red on red hides the warnings.

Keep: the pixel office-horror look and humour, the sniper’s red laser (“the best tell in the game”), the fast first minute.

What playtesting with agents taught us

The orchestrator found the worst bug first

Calibration surfaced the stalled wave before any persona played.

Persona claims need checking

Of six claims: three design flaws, two harness artefacts, one bot limit.

Damage sources beat deaths as evidence

Naming every hit like a player would made “what killed me” the most-used evidence.

No choice screens is no blocker

Exposing the bot’s tactics gave personas something real to decide.

Open the round 1 report →

What still breaks

Agents say “done” without proof

That’s why the factory has a review gate and a “tests not run” line.

Long runs fill the context window

Reliability drops as it fills. Subagents keep the big reads out of the main window; /clear between tasks.

An instruction is not a guarantee

CLAUDE.md is read, not enforced. Anything that must never happen needs a guardrail outside the model.

A factory amplifies the spec it gets

Skip the alignment phase and it builds the wrong thing faster, five times in a row.

Staying in charge without reading the code

The workflow is a dial, and you set it per project.

Every gate manual

You read the design, answer the grill, review the code yourself.

Only the functional check

You try the result. Review skills do the rest.

Their worry

Where do the decisions live?

In the grill and the spec. Written down before a line of code exists. Buildwise: DECISIONS.md.

Their worry

How do I follow a change?

A ticket goes in, a report comes out. You read the report, not the diff. The OVERTIME page was exactly that.

Their worry

What stops spaghetti?

Review skills built on standards you wrote once. Tests the hook won’t let it skip. Applied every run, by something that doesn’t get tired.

The human

When do I still decide?

What it should look like. What each ticket means. Whether it works. Those three gates never move, whatever the dial says.

Without reading the code you never get to 100%. This gets you to 90%, and you were at 0%.

All of it together: one orchestrator, a team of subagents, and you at two gates.

Overkill for a game. The right shape for a real project.

Every stage is a skill. Every subagent is one Agent call. You sit at the two gates where judgment matters: what it should look like, and what each ticket means.

Monday morning

Everyone

Pick one task you’d normally just type into the box. Ask Claude to grill you first, and don’t let it start until it has nothing left to ask.

Developers

Write the CLAUDE.md for one repository: the commands, the conventions, where the tests live.

Teams

Practise the factory on something low-stakes first. Then point it at a real ticket, in manual mode.

The better you know the car, the further you can let it drive.
